title: Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered.
gist: Jessica Hamzelou surveys the expanding pet-preservation market (longevity drugs, cloning at $50,000, cryonics) and says she would use drugs for health but rejects cloning and cryonics, arguing pet loss teaches children that death is final and that cryonic revival chances are near zero.

insights.claim: A growing number of biotech companies target pet longevity, including Loyal, which is working on three potential longevity drugs for dogs and trialing one for metabolic health in about 1,300 pet dogs across the US.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Veterinary longevity is an active venture-funded niche; trial readouts are catalysts to watch.

insights.claim: Other companies are testing dog drugs aimed at age-related conditions such as obesity and osteoarthritis and at aging itself, and one company focuses on longevity medicines for domesticated cats.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Pet drugs may serve as a lower-barrier testbed for aging therapeutics.

insights.claim: Viagen Pets offers to clone cats and dogs for $50,000 each, producing a genetic twin rather than an exact replica, and markets itself as offering customers “a way to hold on.”
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: A priced consumer biotech service showing willingness to pay for emotional continuity.

insights.claim: Alcor, a cryonics facility in Arizona, stores the remains of hundreds of pets as well as people and recently announced it cooled its first pet sugar glider.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Pet cryonics is a small but real revenue line for cryonics providers.

insights.claim: Hamzelou argues the chances of being reunited with a pet through cryonics are bordering on zero, and even people in the field acknowledge stored animals are unlikely to be reanimated, so there is currently no way to truly bring an animal back.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Cryonics offers emotional rather than technical value; set expectations accordingly.
insights.quote: With cryonics, the chances of being reunited with your pet are bordering on zero.

insights.claim: Animal-human relationship researcher Lori Kogan sees no problem with cloning a pet, noting that unlike the loss of a person, pet loss lacks established rituals and can cause isolating disenfranchised grief.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Underserved grief support is the demand-side explanation for the pet-cloning market.

insights.claim: The author argues pet loss in childhood is often a child's first confrontation with death and is formative, and she would not want her children to believe individuals can be replicated, replaced or revived.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Ethical pushback that could shape consumer sentiment toward cloning and cryonics.
